{{Use American English|date=June 2026}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=June 2026}}
A '''Public Use Microdata Area''' (PUMA) is a geographic unit used by the [[US Census]] for providing statistical and demographic information. Each PUMA contains at least 100,000 people. PUMAs do not overlap, and are contained within a single [[U.S. state|state]]. PUMAs were first created for the [[1990 United States census|1990 Census]].<ref>{{cite web|title=2010 Public Use Microdata Areas (PUMAs)  and Characteristics of Microdata|url=https://www.census.gov/geo/reference/pdfs/puma/puma_tutorial.pdf|publisher=U.S. Census Bureau|accessdate=23 October 2013}}</ref> {{As of|2022|post=,}} based on the results of the [[2020 United States census|2020 Census]], there are 2,487 PUMAs.

PUMAs allow the Census to publish census data for sub-state areas throughout every state. For example, the ACS publishes detailed data every year, but due to their sampling procedure only publishes data for census area that have more than 65,000 People. Only seven of the 55 counties of West Virginia were large enough to receive estimates from the 2006 ACS. In contrast, all 12 PUMAs that partition West Virginia received 2006 ACS estimates.

The state governments drew PUMA boundaries for the [[2000 United States census|2000 Census]], to allow reporting of detailed data for all areas. There were a total of 2,071 PUMAs in the 2000 Census.
